narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 58.9% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Your rejection was driven primarily by three pieces of information, ranked by importance. The single strongest factor was your LSAT score of 22.5, which is substantially below the average of 37.2 among students who were accepted. This low score pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.90 was the second most important factor. Although it pulled the prediction slightly in a more positive direction, the improvement was modest because the score remains noticeably below the 3.23 average of accepted students. Finally, your middle family income bracket contributed a small additional nudge toward passing; however, this effect was far weaker than the impact of your test scores and grades.

Taken together, the model concluded that the combination of a low LSAT and below-average grades created too high a risk of bar exam failure, outweighing the modest positive signal from your family background.

You should focus on raising your LSAT score through targeted preparation, as this was the dominant reason for the rejection. Retaking the exam with a significantly higher result, combined with any further improvement in your academic record, would substantially improve your chances on a future application.
